title: A Fire in a Bihar Hospital's ICU Killed at Least Four People. The Staff Had Already Fled.
excerpt: A short circuit at Prasad Hospital in Muzaffarpur turned the intensive care unit into a death trap. Families say doctors abandoned patients as smoke filled the building.
body:
A fire broke out in the intensive care unit of Prasad Hospital in Bihar's Muzaffarpur district in the early hours of Thursday, killing at least four people and injuring more than twenty. The blaze, believed to have been caused by a short circuit, spread rapidly through the fifth-floor ICU, filling it with thick, toxic smoke before most patients could be moved.

The hospital is one of the largest private healthcare facilities in North Bihar. At the time of the fire, around 15 patients were in the ICU, many of them on ventilators or otherwise immobile.

Rescue workers, including local residents who arrived before fire tenders, pulled 58 people from the building. Twenty-one were declared dead on arrival at other hospitals. Officials have cautioned that the toll could rise, with several of the injured in critical condition.

## Staff Vanished Before the Fire Trucks Arrived

The most damning allegation comes from family members of the patients. Multiple witnesses told local reporters that doctors and hospital staff fled the building after the fire broke out, leaving critically ill patients trapped in the ICU.

A fire department official confirmed that most hospital staff were absent when emergency responders arrived. Families accused police of hurriedly removing bodies from the site. One nurse was accused of initially claiming that some of the deceased were still alive — an allegation that has not been independently verified.

The ICU in-charge of Prasad Hospital was seriously injured in the fire and is being treated at another facility. Whether the injury came from attempting to help patients or during the evacuation remains unclear.

## The Pattern That Keeps Repeating

The Muzaffarpur fire comes just a day after 21 people died in a fire at a hotel in Delhi's Malviya Nagar, where foreign nationals who had come to India for medical treatment were among the victims. That fire, too, raised questions about emergency protocols, fire safety compliance, and the speed of official response.

India loses more people to building fires than almost any other country. The National Crime Records Bureau reported over 17,000 fire-related deaths in 2023, many of them in hospitals, hotels, and factories where safety norms are routinely flouted.

In Bihar, fire safety compliance has been a persistent problem. A 2024 audit by the state fire department found that fewer than 40 per cent of private hospitals in the state had functional fire safety systems, including sprinklers, fire alarms, and marked evacuation routes. Many operated without the mandatory no-objection certificate from the fire department.

Prasad Hospital's compliance status has not yet been disclosed. Muzaffarpur District Magistrate Subrat Kumar Sen said strict action would follow if negligence was established. "The ICU had around 15 patients at the time of the fire. Some family members have alleged that their patients are missing. Every aspect of the incident is being investigated," he said.

## What It Means for Medical Tourism

The back-to-back tragedies — Delhi and now Muzaffarpur — arrive at a particularly sensitive moment for India's medical tourism industry. The Delhi hotel fire killed foreign patients who had travelled to India for affordable healthcare, a sector the government has been aggressively promoting.

India's medical tourism market is projected to reach $13 billion by 2027, driven by low-cost procedures and a growing network of internationally accredited hospitals. But the country's fire safety infrastructure has not kept pace with the ambition. International accreditation bodies like JCI and NABH mandate fire safety compliance, but the vast majority of India's private hospitals — particularly those outside the top cities — operate without such accreditation.

The diaspora, which often arranges medical care in India for elderly parents and relatives, has particular reason to pay attention. The question is not whether India's doctors are skilled — they are. The question is whether the buildings they work in will keep patients alive long enough to be treated.

Residents of Muzaffarpur have asked the most basic of questions: whether a timely water supply and a faster response could have reduced the casualties. In a city where the nearest fire station is equipped with aging engines and limited manpower, the answer may be one no official wants to give.
author: Diaspora Desk
